title: Runbook: Stability Explorations and Chaos Sampling for Throughput Benchmarks
content:
Purpose:
This runbook collects pragmatic guidance for running stability-focused throughput experiments: how to systematically introduce noise/chaos, pick sampling points, and judge when a run is repeatable enough to be a canonical measurement. It is intentionally operational: checklists, quick diagnostics, and known failure modes.

Scope and motivation:
- We already have repeatable ramp/plateau benchmark playbooks; this doc focuses on the *exploratory* layer: resilience to microbursts, background noise, scheduling jitter, and thermal/CPU/GPU contention.
- Goal: reduce surprises in customer-facing tail latency and throughput regressions by rooting out fragile operating points early.
- Audience: SREs running long validation campaigns, serving-runtime engineers prototyping kernel changes, and performance owners validating build candidates.

Quick overview of experiment families:
1) Deterministic stability sweep
   - Controlled ramp to target qps, hold for X minutes, then step up. No injected noise. Purpose: baseline repeatability and resource occupancy curve.
2) Chaos-sampled bursts
   - Add randomized microbursts on top of baseline (Poisson or Pareto arrivals) to probe queueing transparency and batching collapse. Useful to find burst amplification points.
3) Background contention replay
   - Simulate noisy co-tenants: synthetic background processes (CPU/GPU memcpy stress, disk IO, kernel interrupt storms). Assess graceful degradation and backpressure behavior.
4) N-1 and node eviction tests
   - Remove a serving process or GPU mid-run to validate auto-recovery, cold-cache impact, and circuit-breakers.
5) Long-run drift detection
   - Multi-hour runs to catch thermal throttling, memory fragmentation, and scheduler degeneracy.

Load profile primitives (building blocks):
- staircase: linear steps (e.g., 20 -> 40 -> 60 qps) with hold periods
- plateau: ramp to target then hold for stabilization window
- microburst: short (100-1000ms) high-qps spikes inserted at randomized intervals
- jittered-poisson: base arrival with randomized inter-arrival per lambda
- occupancy-probe: fixed sequence-length mixes to stress KV cache and batching

Warmup and stabilization heuristics (operational):
- Warmup goal: ensure all caches (model weights, KV caches, memory allocators) reach representative steady behavior.
- Heuristic A (fast): run plateau for min(2 minutes, 3*median latency sample) then check metrics for 60s window.
- Heuristic B (robust): require 3 consecutive 60s windows where token-rate, p95 latency, and batching efficiency change < 2% between windows. Only then mark stabilized.
- If warmup fails after 10 minutes, automatically capture a debugging trace and abort.

Stabilization detection algorithm (pseudo):
- Collect metrics every 5s: tokens/sec, p50/p95/p99 latency, avg batch size, GPU utilization, cpu_steal
- For each metric compute rolling mean and coefficient-of-variation (CoV) over last N=12 samples.
- Consider metric stable if CoV < 0.02 for all critical signals for T_stable = 3 consecutive windows.
- If stable, start canonical capture; otherwise extend warmup or reduce load and retry.

Metrics to capture (minimum):
- Client-visible: requests/s, tokens/s, p50/p90/p95/p99 latencies, error rate (4xx/5xx), response size distribution.
- Runtime internals: avg batch size, KV cache hit ratio, queue length, scheduling latency, context-switch rate.
- Host/GPU: GPU util, SM occupancy, GPU memory allocated/free, PCIe bandwidth, CPU user/sys/idle/steal, thermal sensors, power draw if available.
- System: disk IO, network packets/sec, socket queue lengths.
- Traces: distributed spans for slow requests including kernel counts and stall reasons.

Sampling and repeatability guidance:
- Deterministic seeds: provide a reproducible request set (fixed prompts, deterministic RNG seeds, and fixed sequence-length distribution). Store the seed and hash of the request corpus with the run.
- Anchors: include 5 short canonical 'anchor' requests at low concurrency every 2 minutes to verify functional parity and avoid silent model drift.
- Sampling windows: prefer 60–120s canonical windows for primary measurements. For microburst analysis, collect sub-windowed samples at 1s resolution.
- Run N=5 independent repeats for any candidate comparison; report mean and confidence intervals. If variance > 5% on tokens/sec across repeats, escalate to diagnosis run (longer warmup, tighter anchors).

Chaos sampling strategies (how to add noise):
- Microburst generator parameters: burst_length_ms {200, 500, 1000}, burst_qps_multiplier {2x, 5x, 10x}, inter_burst_dist {exponential, fixed-interval, Pareto-heavy-tail}.
- Node eviction: randomly pick a serving replica and drain/kill process at a random time in hold window. Observe cold-cache impact and failover latencies.
- Background load: add configurable GPU memcpy loops and host CPU stress threads; scale intensity until 10% degradation baseline observed — then back off.
- Network perturbations: add egress latency and packet loss at the proxy layer to emulate cross-region flakiness.

Data collection and artifacts per run:
- Prometheus snapshot (raw series) covering test window plus 5 minutes before/after.
- Load generator log (per-request timing, request metadata, seed).
- Perf/tram/NSYS profiles for representative slow requests (if available).
- Short perf ring buffer for kernel-level anomalies.
- A JSON summary with run parameters and stabilized/not flag and hashes of corpora.

Known pitfalls and mitigations:
- Batching collapse: sudden microbursts may flush queued requests into many small batches — look for avg_batch_size drop and p99 spike. Mitigation: introduce pacing gate or microburst smoothing at loadgen-side or increase batching window conservatively.
- Cold-cache amplification: evicting nodes mid-run amplifies latency; ensure we capture both immediate and steady-state after rejoin. Use anchors to detect functional/regression blips.
- Thermal drift: long runs on packed GPUs can show slowly increasing latency; add thermal sensors to run dashboard and correlate with tokens/sec.
- Non-deterministic loadgen: jitter in client machines (SYS load, NTP drift) can masquerade as instability — dedicate a clean loadgen VM or container and isolate CPU quotas.

Run checklist (preflight):
1) Verify request corpus hash and seed documented.
2) Ensure loadgen VM is pinned (CPU isolate) and time-synced.
3) Confirm metric scraping endpoints reachable and retention window >= run duration + 1 hour.
4) Confirm tracing/troubleshooting hooks enabled for slow requests.
5) Reserve GPUs/nodes for the run (avoid noisy neighbors) unless test explicitly requires contention.
6) Start background recording (nsys/perf) for a sampling set of requests.
7) Kick off warmup, monitor stabilization algorithm, capture stabilized flag.

Quick triage guide (when run shows high variance):
- Step 1: Check loadgen logs and anchors for request-level anomalies. If anchors fail, the test corpus or orchestration likely at fault.
- Step 2: Check avg_batch_size and queue length trends — sudden dips point to batching collapse.
- Step 3: Inspect GPU SM utilization and PCIe stalls — increased memory pressure often visible here.
- Step 4: Look at host-level cpu_steal and context-switch spikes — scheduling issues.
- Step 5: If unresolved, reproduce a shorter window with heavier tracing and node-local perf sampling.

Example loadgen snippets (notes to runner):
- Staircase baseline (bash pseudo):
  ./loadgen --profile staircase --steps "20:300,40:300,60:600" --seed 42 --request-corpus requests-v2.json --out summary.json
- Microburst overlay (bash pseudo):
  ./loadgen --profile plateau --qps 50 --burst "type=pareto,length_ms=500,multiplier=8,rate=0.03" --seed 31415 
    --anchors anchors.json --metrics-prom-url $PROM

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How fine should stabilization thresholds be when evaluating kernel-level changes that reduce latency by <2%? (trade-off cost/time).
- Can we formalize an adaptive warmup that shortens once a change proves low-variance historically?
- Investigate adding an automated batch-size anomaly detector that can flag likely batching collapse during runs.

Appendix: example JSON schema for canonical summary (flat map):
- run_id, model, variant, qps_profile, seed, stabilized_flag, tokens_per_sec_median, tokens_per_sec_cov, p95_latency_ms_median, avg_batch_size_median, artifacts: [prom_snapshot, loadgen_log, perf_samples]
(we store this as a simple flat JSON file per run in the artifacts bucket).

Notes to self / ephemeral ideas:
- Try mixing in small proportion (5%) of very long-sequence requests during plateau to exercise KV eviction behavior.
- Consider a short-lived "batching window" knob on the runtime for experiments to measure sensitivity.
- Add test tag that automatically triggers a follow-up run if variance threshold exceeded.

References and helpful links:
- Confluence page (design notes): https://confluence.redwood.ai/pages/DEV-RT-CHAOS
- Jira epic: JIRA-RT-4523 (stability sweeps)
- Example PR with instrumentation changes: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/981

Status: draft operational runbook, intended to be iterated after the next two validation campaigns.
summary: Operational runbook for running stability/chaos experiments against the serving runtime: sampling strategies, warmup heuristics, metrics, checklists, and triage guidance.
